learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected a middling total value and locked the prediction for the allocation reached by raising prices on over-wanted houses.
observations.exploration: Pressed Raise twice. House a rose to 1 then 2; buyer y shifted toward b and buyer z tied a and b. Ran to round 3, with prices a 3, b 1, c 0 and allocation x-a, y-c, z-b, total 23. Compared all six matches: totals 21, 23, 14, 17, 15 and 16.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to highest total, accurately described three raises and the final joint rise of a and b, and linked clearing prices to the best match. It generalized existence and highest total value to other values and disclosed invented data.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot after Compare. A 3 by 3 value-minus-price grid showed wanted cells and selected assignments; the winning 23 chip was highlighted among six possible matches. Price labels and round total were readable, though the many marks required attention.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question distinguishes decentralized choices from total allocation quality.
prediction.evidence: Selected a middling outcome before running the price process.

interaction.reason: Price steps expose changing preferred options and a final comparison against all alternatives.
interaction.evidence: Two manual raises, one run step and six totals established the observed winner.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the over-demanded group and accurately summarizes the path.
payoff.evidence: It described the joint a and b rise and final total 23.

clarity.reason: The dense grid asks the learner to track values, prices, net values, wants and assignments at once.
clarity.evidence: Dots, outlines, fills and six compact assignment chips share the panel.

transfer.reason: The generalization is stated but no new values or allocation case can be tried.
transfer.evidence: The ending says the result holds for any values, while the toy stays fixed.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Local price responses produce the highest of six total values.
surprise.evidence: The observed 23 exceeded every compared alternative despite z preferring a before price.

visualExplanation.reason: The grid shows how prices change net preferences and resolve conflicts.
visualExplanation.evidence: At round 3, y wanted b or c and z wanted a or b, allowing separate choices.

playfulness.reason: Step and run controls support investigation, but the puzzle is largely predetermined.
playfulness.evidence: Only the fixed price process and comparison are available.

practicalValue.reason: It gives intuition for prices as coordination signals.
practicalValue.evidence: Prices rose on over-wanted groups until distinct wanted houses could be assigned.

depth.reason: The lesson includes group over-demand and comparison with the full small solution space.
depth.evidence: The final raise includes a and b together, beyond a simple individual price story.

complexity.reason: The control count is small, but interpreting the multi-layer matching process requires sustained attention.
complexity.conceptualDemand: High: coordinate individual net preferences, group over-demand and total raw value.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Moderate: four buttons are simple, but the matrix has multiple simultaneous encodings.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: A price-adjusted individual choice can support a globally best raw-value matching.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Market clearing, matching and over-demanded groups are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: High: 3 by 3 arithmetic grid, prices, desire marks, assignment marks and compact match codes.

whyCool: Raising only contested prices sorts conflicting preferences into the best small matching without directly optimizing the displayed total.
caveat: The general theorem is asserted after one fixed invented example; no new value matrix or proof is explored.
missingEvidence: No fresh assignment values were tested.
